correction.textOverride: For each objective probability—from one percent to 100 percent—we wants to know the subjective probability weight. When we make decisions, do we treats a one-percent chance just like one percent, or like something else? Events that could happen but aren’t likely—low-probability events—can define as probabilities up to about 25 percent. Low-probability events tends to factor more into decisions than they should. That is, an event that has an objective one-percent chance of occurring could subjective seem like it has a five-percent chance of occurring. We underestimate the likelihood of these low-probability events. In general, the smaller the probability, the most we overestimate its likelihood. For example, people who play the lottery is often optimistic about winning. However, the odds of a single ticket winning the largest, most popular U.S. lotteries is on the order of one in 175 million.
